This morning is proposed amendments to the Water Works bylaw.
The City of Saskatoon is proposing amendments to bylaw number 7567, the Water Works bylaw.
To enhance operational safety, improve efficiency and align with recent council decisions, particularly regarding the advanced metering infrastructure or AMI program.

He changes include updating water meter installation standards, improving cross-connection controls to protect public health and delegating authority to the administration for revising technical specifications on all meter sizes.
These updates aimed to streamline communication with developers and contractors by consolidating design standards within the city's design and development standards manual website.

Additional amendments address the mandatory participation in the AMI program requiring AMI meters in all new commercial and industrial properties and introducing cost recovery provisions for damaged or disposed AMI equipment.
Previously, the city absorbed these costs, but the proposed changes would shift responsibility to property owners similar to traditional water meter policies.
The report also recommends updates to definitions and terminology for clarity and consistency.
If approved, the city solicitor will draft the necessary bylaw revisions with final approval anticipated in early 2026.

This first information report is to provide an update on the waterworks program and the evaluation
of project delivery models, specifically the introduction of construction management at risk
procurement method.
So referred to a CMAR.
Earlier this year, City Council approved the detailed funding plan for the water treatment
long-term capital strategy.
That report indicated that CMAR was identified as the preferred delivery method for the
waterworks program.
A smaller scale trial project at the existing water treatment plan will test CMAR before
decision is made on its use for the new plant.
CMAR involves hiring a designer and a construction manager under separate contracts near
the beginning of the project.
The construction manager is engaged early in the design phase to provide input on constructability,
cost and scheduling.
Once the design is finalized, negotiations with the contractor on the cost and schedule
are completed.
And if an agreement has reached, the project proceeds to construction.
If we are unable at that time to come to an agreement with the contractor on price or schedule,
the project will revert to a traditional design bid build procurement method.
The report outlines many benefits of CMAR, some of which include early contractor involvement
to improve the quality of the design, cost certainty as adjustments to design and constructability
are considered before pricing is finalized.
The risks are identified early and assigned appropriately between the parties.
More collaboration between the consultants, the contractor and our project team in the early stages
of the project reduces delays and redesigns.
And lastly, transparency, CMAR uses open book pricing and independent cost validation to ensure
we are getting the best value for our investments.
The report does also identify a few challenges with the introduction of CMAR, including the
requirement for more upfront effort and internal resources, the shift from low bid to qualifications
based procurement.
So in the end, we may pay a bit more for an overall project, but we get a better overall
product in the end.
To that effect, there may be some additional design phase costs, but potential savings
during construction.
And in the end, if no agreement is reached with the contractor on the price and scheduling
after completion of the design and planning work, the project may face some minor delays
transitioning to a different procurement method.
We are currently in the process of awarding the design contract and pre-qualifying contractors.
An RFP for the construction manager is intended to be issued before the end of this year,
if the construction manager expected to be in place by early 2026.
The next steps will be to deliver the CMAR trial project and evaluate its effectiveness
in order to make a decision on the delivery method for the new water treatment plant.
